seoDescription: Harmed by a doctor, hospital, or clinic in Dearborn? Michigan malpractice law has a two-year deadline, a 182-day notice before suit, a sworn expert affidavit, and a cap on pain-and-suffering damages ($596,400 or $1,065,000 in 2026). ATLAW’s Dearborn office explains the rules, Corewell Health Dearborn and the city’s clinics, and the different path for federally funded providers. Free review in English or Arabic. (313) 406-7606.
tagline: Michigan gives a malpractice victim two years, not three, and requires a notice and an expert’s affidavit before the case can be filed. In Dearborn the defendant may be the hospital on Oakwood Boulevard, a Michigan Avenue clinic, a federally funded health center, or the City’s EMS, and each has its own rules.

c.v: Michigan has built more procedural requirements into medical malpractice claims than into any other kind of injury case: a two-year deadline instead of three, a written notice to each provider 182 days before suit, a sworn affidavit from a qualified expert filed with the complaint, strict rules about who that expert can be, and a cap on pain-and-suffering damages.

Dearborn adds a question of its own: who the defendant is. The hospital on Oakwood Boulevard is a private nonprofit. The clinic on Michigan Avenue may be a physician group, a hospital-owned practice, or a federally funded community health center whose providers can only be sued under federal law. The ambulance was the City’s. And a patient who was treated through an interpreter, or without one, has a consent question the record must answer.

sections.heading: What malpractice is, and is not

c.v: A bad outcome is not malpractice. Malpractice is a bad outcome caused by a provider who failed to do what a reasonably competent provider in the same specialty would have done in the same circumstances (MCL 600.2912a). You must prove the standard of care, a breach, that the breach more likely than not caused the injury, and damages; Michigan requires proof that the patient would have had a better outcome, not merely a chance of one (MCL 600.2912a(2)). A qualified physician’s written review of the records decides, before anything is filed, whether a case exists. Many do not, and we say so.

sections.heading: Dearborn’s providers, and who answers for each

c.v: The city’s hospital, on Oakwood Boulevard, formerly Beaumont Dearborn and before that Oakwood Hospital, now part of Corewell Health, a private nonprofit. Emergency department, surgical, obstetric, and inpatient claims against the hospital and its employed providers proceed in the Third Judicial Circuit Court under the Michigan rules above. Physicians who practice there may be hospital employees or independent groups, and the employer must be identified before the Notice of Intent is served.

Henry Ford Health’s medical center on Hubbard Drive at Fairlane and the many independent and hospital-owned practices along Michigan Avenue, Ford Road, and Outer Drive. Private; Michigan rules apply. A delayed diagnosis in a primary-care or specialty office is the common Dearborn claim.

Several health centers serving Dearborn receive federal Health Center Program funding, and their employed providers are deemed federal employees for malpractice purposes. A claim against one follows the Federal Tort Claims Act, not Michigan procedure: an administrative claim on Standard Form 95 to the Department of Health and Human Services within two years (28 USC 2401(b)), no Notice of Intent, suit in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan tried to a judge without a jury, with Michigan substantive law and caps applied. Identifying a deemed clinic early is the difference between a timely claim and none.

A large share of Dearborn patients speak Arabic at home. Hospitals and clinics that receive federal funds must provide meaningful language access, and informed consent obtained from a patient who could not understand the explanation is a consent the record must justify. Where a procedure’s material risks were never explained in a language the patient understood, the consent claim is part of the malpractice case.

faqs.question: How long do I have to sue a Dearborn doctor or hospital?

answer.v: Two years from the malpractice, with a six-month discovery rule capped at six years. Because the Notice of Intent must be served 182 days before suit and the expert review comes first, call well inside the first year.

faqs.question: My care was at a community health center in Dearborn. Is that different?

answer.v: It may be. If the center is federally funded and its providers are deemed federal employees, the claim is against the United States under the Federal Tort Claims Act: an administrative claim within two years, no Notice of Intent, and suit in federal court without a jury. We check the center’s status at the first call.

faqs.question: Is there a cap on what I can recover?

answer.v: On pain-and-suffering damages only: $596,400 for most cases and $1,065,000 for the most severe permanent injuries in 2026, adjusted each January. Medical bills, lost earnings, and future care are not capped.

faqs.question: I signed a consent form I could not read. Does that matter?

answer.v: It can. Consent must be informed, and a form signed without an explanation the patient could understand, in a language the patient speaks, may not be. The record of what was explained, and how, is part of the case.

faqs.question: My child was injured at birth at a Dearborn hospital. How long do we have?

answer.v: A child injured before age eight has until the tenth birthday to file. The parents’ own claims are subject to the ordinary two-year period, so the family should not wait.

faqs.question: Do I need a Notice of Intent?

answer.v: Yes, for any Michigan provider: a written notice served on each defendant at least 182 days before filing, stating the standard of care, the breach, and causation. Serving it on time pauses the two-year clock during the waiting period.
